question: Can a pretrained one-hidden-layer MLP or gated linear unit be converted analytically into its least-squares-optimal polynomial surrogate under a Gaussian or Gaussian-mixture input model, enabling spectral interpretation of ordinary nonlinear weights?

key_findings.claim: For Gaussian inputs, the paper derives exact linear least-squares coefficients for a one-hidden-layer MLP from activation moments and Stein's lemma.
key_findings.evidence: Ordinary least squares gives beta=Cov[x]^{-1}Cov[f(x),x] and an intercept from the means. Linear transformations make each preactivation Gaussian; ReLU and GELU means and expected derivatives have analytic formulas, while other elementwise activations can be integrated with Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Stein's lemma reduces the cross-moment E[activation(y_i)x_j] to a covariance times E[activation'(y_i)].

key_findings.claim: A master identity reduces polynomial cross-moments involving a nonlinear Gaussian preactivation to one-dimensional integrals.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 rewrites E[g(X) product_i Y_i] as a degree-n combination of E[g(X)X^k]. It regresses each jointly Gaussian Y_i on X, uses independence of the Gaussian residuals from X, expands the product combinatorially, and evaluates residual products with Isserlis' theorem. This supplies the cross-covariances needed after lifting x to linear and quadratic monomials and extends formally to arbitrary polynomial degree.

key_findings.claim: The framework covers Gaussian mixtures and GLUs algebraically, but tractability sharply limits the promised closed-form conversion.
key_findings.evidence: Mixture moments are combined with the law of total covariance, and each GLU output reduces to E[activation(Y_i)Z_i] with jointly Gaussian variables. Yet a degree-n approximant requires O(d*k^n) coefficients. Even MNIST's 784-dimensional quadratic lift has 307,720 features and a covariance matrix with 94.7 billion entries; the paper therefore cannot compute its class-mixture quadratic in closed form and instead initializes from a standard-Gaussian solution and fine-tunes with SGD.

anchors.section: Appendix B, O(d^6) quadratic solve and SGD fine-tuning

key_findings.claim: On one MNIST ReLU MLP, the surrogate trajectory is consistent with a shift from linear to predominantly quadratic behavior during training.
key_findings.evidence: For checkpoints evaluated on a class-conditional Gaussian mixture matching MNIST moments, linear fraction of variance unexplained rises sharply between 500 and 1,000 steps and continues to about 4,000, whereas quadratic FVU remains nearly constant and final quadratic R-squared exceeds 95%. Both FVUs initially decrease, but that early simplification disappears under KL divergence. The evidence is thus metric-dependent and does not distinguish quadratic computation from other nonlinear functions that happen to project well onto degree two.

key_findings.claim: Spectral components of the surrogate identify directions causally important to the original classifier, although the intervention is conspicuous rather than a standard small-perturbation attack.
key_findings.evidence: The authors take the SVD of the linear coefficient matrix and project every test image away from its top left-singular directions. Original and surrogate accuracies fall together; removing four components drops the ReLU MLP below 50%, and removing all ten output-row-space directions brings it near chance while digits remain qualitatively recognizable. The transformation is a dataset-wide rank-k projection with no norm or perceptual budget, so it demonstrates causal subspace transfer rather than imperceptible adversarial vulnerability.

key_findings.claim: The empirical study does not yet validate polynomial conversion as an interpretability method for the Transformer MLPs and GLUs motivating the work.
key_findings.evidence: All reported approximation, feature-visualization, training-dynamics, and intervention experiments use a single-hidden-layer ReLU network on MNIST. Transformer residual streams, modern SwiGLUs, multiple layers, language tokens, and natural-data activation distributions are explicitly left as future work. The proposed route—eigendecomposing a quadratic Transformer-FFN surrogate into an overcomplete residual-stream basis—is conjectural in this paper.

method.core_idea: Project a feedforward module onto low-degree monomials under a maximum-entropy Gaussian input model, then interpret the resulting linear maps and quadratic forms with SVD or eigendecomposition.
method.mechanism: Specify input mean and covariance, optionally per mixture component. Propagate those moments through the first affine layer so every preactivation is Gaussian. Evaluate activation, derivative, and higher cross-moments analytically for ReLU/GELU or numerically in one dimension. Construct the ordinary-least-squares covariance and cross-covariance matrices for monomial features, solve for polynomial coefficients, and combine mixture components by total covariance. For GLUs, include the second linear gate in the joint-Gaussian moments. Diagnose fidelity with FVU/KL and interpret low-degree coefficients spectrally.
assumptions: The module is a one-hidden-layer MLP or GLU with an elementwise activation and affine projections.
Inputs are Gaussian or are adequately represented by a finite Gaussian mixture with known means, covariances, and weights.
Least-squares fidelity under that reference distribution is relevant to the model's real activation distribution and behavioral mechanism.
Low-degree coefficients fit in memory and their covariance linear system can be solved stably.
High output R-squared is sufficient for spectral features and interventions to transfer to the original nonlinear module.
Eigenvectors or singular vectors of the coefficients correspond to human-meaningful features rather than arbitrary rotations or dataset artifacts.
The surrogate's global Gaussian behavior is a useful guard against training-sample overfitting rather than an unrealistic source of off-manifold directions.
A phase change in linear-versus-quadratic approximation error reflects increasing learned statistical order.

techniques.role: Computes distribution-optimal polynomial coefficients from analytic moments instead of sampling and regression.
Turns activation-input cross-covariances into expected activation derivatives under a univariate Gaussian.
Reduces nonlinear multivariate Gaussian product moments to a sum of one-dimensional moments.
Combines component-level moments into a single least-squares surrogate for class-conditional data.
Extracts high-magnitude interaction directions from output-specific quadratic coefficient matrices.
Projects inputs away from directions selected by the linear surrogate to test causal transfer.
Tracks linear and quadratic FVU or KL over training as a proxy for functional complexity.

evaluations.setting: Single-hidden-layer ReLU MLP trained on MNIST with schedule-free AdamW and log-spaced checkpoints
evaluations.metric: Linear and quadratic fraction of variance unexplained on a moment-matched Gaussian mixture
evaluations.result: Linear FVU rises sharply after roughly 500-1,000 steps while quadratic FVU remains nearly constant; the final quadratic surrogate explains over 95% of output variance

evaluations.setting: Same MNIST checkpoints and Gaussian-mixture evaluation distribution
evaluations.metric: KL divergence between classifier output distributions
evaluations.result: The later linear-versus-quadratic trend resembles FVU, but the early decrease in both FVU curves disappears under KL

evaluations.setting: Extra-long MNIST training run with class-specific polynomial coefficient visualization
evaluations.metric: Qualitative linear maps and leading quadratic eigenvectors over checkpoints
evaluations.result: Digit-like structure is clearest in intermediate checkpoints and later acquires artifacts as the network overfits

evaluations.setting: Dataset-wide SVD projections applied to MNIST test inputs
evaluations.metric: Accuracy of the original ReLU MLP and its polynomial surrogates as one to ten directions are removed
evaluations.result: All accuracies decline together; four removed directions lower the MLP below 50% and ten lower it near chance while digits remain visually recognizable
evaluations.baseline: Unmodified test set and different numbers of ablated singular directions

limitations: Author-stated: analytic derivations assume Gaussian-mixture inputs and may not generalize usefully to other distributions; data-distribution fine-tuning is suggested when the assumption is too restrictive.
Author-stated: degree-n coefficients require d*k^n storage, making degree two the practical ceiling for tens-of-thousands-dimensional activations.
Author-stated: when a quadratic surrogate has poor fidelity, the proposed spectral interpretation cannot be used reliably in isolation.
Reviewer-identified: the only empirical network is a shallow MNIST ReLU classifier; there is no Transformer, language, GLU, deep-MLP, or realistic residual-stream validation.

Reviewer-identified: the MNIST Gaussian-mixture quadratic is itself computationally intractable, so the headline closed-form method is replaced by standard-Gaussian initialization plus SGD in the main nonlinear experiment.

Reviewer-identified: matching means and covariances does not establish that Gaussian surrogates preserve higher-order manifold structure, tails, sparsity, token conditioning, or causal feature prevalence.
Reviewer-identified: high R-squared is an average-output metric and can coexist with severe errors on rare, safety-relevant, class-boundary, or out-of-distribution inputs.

Reviewer-identified: the increasing-degree interpretation is not identified causally; a higher-degree or nonpolynomial function can change its best linear projection while the quadratic projection stays stable.
Reviewer-identified: the initial simplification appears under FVU but not KL, showing that the claimed training phases depend on metric and output parameterization.

Reviewer-identified: SVD projection removes up to a ten-dimensional classifier row space with no perturbation budget, random-subspace control, or perceptual metric; it is not comparable to conventional adversarial examples.

Reviewer-identified: eigenvectors of dense quadratic matrices are rotation-sensitive and not automatically monosemantic; the paper offers visual inspection but no human or automated interpretability evaluation.
Reviewer-identified: arbitrary-degree formulas do not resolve the exponential coefficient count, covariance construction, numerical conditioning, or tensor-decomposition problem that dominates scale.

Reviewer-identified: the maximum-entropy choice is only maximum entropy under specified continuous moment constraints; those constraints still encode a substantive and potentially misleading reference distribution.
failure_modes: Transformer MLP inputs are strongly non-Gaussian or context-conditional, so the globally optimal Gaussian surrogate is inaccurate on actual activations.
Quadratic fidelity is high in aggregate but misses a rare gating interaction that causally determines a safety-critical behavior.
The lifted covariance matrix is too large or ill-conditioned to materialize and invert even before coefficient interpretation.
A Gaussian mixture needs too many components to model activation modes, negating analytic and memory advantages.
Leading eigenvectors mix multiple equally weighted features or rotate unpredictably within a degenerate eigenspace.
An intervention transfers because it deletes generic classifier signal, not because the surrogate recovered a specific model mechanism.
An approximation trained or fine-tuned on empirical samples overfits the chosen probe distribution, reintroducing the data/model ambiguity the analytic reference was meant to avoid.
Higher-degree behavior becomes important after fine-tuning or distribution shift, leaving a previously faithful quadratic surrogate obsolete.
Moment estimation error propagates nonlinearly into high-degree coefficients and creates spurious spectral directions.
FVU or R-squared masks logit errors that become large after softmax, temperature scaling, or composition with downstream layers.
reusable_insights: State the reference distribution as part of every mechanistic surrogate; polynomial coefficients are distribution-dependent even when derived from fixed weights.
Evaluate surrogate fidelity both on the analytic reference and on real activations, counterfactuals, rare slices, and downstream behavior.
Use analytic coefficients as an initialization for structured low-rank fitting rather than materializing a full d-by-d quadratic tensor.
Compare spectral interventions to random and norm-matched subspaces to distinguish mechanism recovery from generic signal deletion.
Track multiple discrepancy metrics over training because apparent simplicity phases may be metric-specific.
Separate algebraic arbitrary-degree existence from computational scalability and report both coefficient and solver complexity.
Resolve degenerate eigenspaces with subspace-level interpretation rather than assigning meaning to individual unstable eigenvectors.
Test whether a surrogate composes through neighboring attention, residual, and normalization operations instead of interpreting an isolated module only.
open_questions: Can low-rank tensor trains, CP decompositions, Kronecker structure, or randomized sketches make quadratic Transformer-FFN surrogates tractable?
How Gaussian are real residual-stream and preactivation distributions conditional on token, layer, language, and context?
Can approximation error be bounded on the empirical distribution from deviations in moments or a divergence from the reference Gaussian mixture?
Do spectral features from a SwiGLU surrogate correspond to SAE features, causal circuits, or human-interpretable concepts in language models?
Which fidelity metric best predicts whether surrogate-derived interventions transfer without collateral behavior change?
Can local or conditional polynomial surrogates preserve rare gating regimes without exploding the number of mixture components?
Does the linear-to-quadratic transition reproduce across seeds, architectures, natural images, language models, and different optimizers?
Can downstream composition turn a low-FVU module surrogate into a high-error end-to-end model, and how should that error propagate?
How can eigenspace interpretability be evaluated quantitatively rather than by visual inspection?

competitive_landscape.title: Bilinear MLPs enable weight-based mechanistic interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: Pearce et al. train bilinear GLUs whose computation is exactly quadratic, so interaction tensors and their eigenvectors come directly from weights and are studied on toy, vision, and language tasks. The reviewed paper instead approximates ordinary ReLU/GELU/GLU modules post hoc, preserving pretrained architectures but making interpretability conditional on reference-distribution fidelity.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks Learn Statistics of Increasing Complexity
competitive_landscape.difference: Belrose et al. test distributional simplicity bias by evaluating networks on maximum-entropy distributions with matched low-order moments and by editing class statistics, including evidence in language models. The reviewed work supplies analytic polynomial projections and a sharper linear-versus-quadratic trajectory on MNIST, but does not extend the empirical result beyond that shallow setting.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Sparse autoencoders learn an overcomplete, sparsely active dictionary from actual model activations and demonstrate finer causal localization on a language-model circuit. Polynomial conversion needs no auxiliary feature-learning model and exposes weight-derived interactions, but assumes an input distribution, scales poorly beyond degree two, and has not yet shown semantic language features.

competitive_landscape.title: PolySAE: Modeling Feature Interactions in Sparse Autoencoders via Polynomial Decoding
competitive_landscape.difference: PolySAE retains sparse learned activation features but augments decoding with polynomial terms to capture compositional interactions, reporting improved probing while avoiding a full dense input polynomial. It targets representation decomposition rather than closed-form approximation of MLP weights and illustrates a scalable hybrid direction between SAE dictionaries and polynomial interactions.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: the paper provides closed-form least-squares-optimal polynomial approximations of arbitrary degree for MLPs and GLUs under Gaussian inputs, enabling weight-oriented spectral interpretation and new evidence for increasing functional complexity during training. Reviewer inference: the master Gaussian-moment reduction and unified MLP/GLU OLS construction are the substantive theoretical contributions. Polynomial interpretable models, Gaussian/Hermite moment methods, bilinear interaction tensors, SAEs, and distributional simplicity bias all predate it. Practical novelty is constrained because even the MNIST quadratic mixture cannot be solved in closed form and all empirical evidence is shallow; the Transformer interpretability use case remains a promising proposal rather than a demonstrated result.
reviewer_notes: All 11 extracted pages were checked, including the linear and quadratic OLS derivations, master theorem, Gaussian-mixture and GLU extensions, complete MNIST protocol, metric-dependent training trajectory, visualizations, SVD intervention, limitations, released-code statement, ReLU/GELU integral formulas, and the O(d^6) implementation bottleneck. Adjacent and competing work was independently checked on primary arXiv, OpenReview, and NeurIPS records through 2026-08-23.
